assets.topic: The Transformative Mask: Anonymity Unhinges Restraint
assets.visual_frame_description: Jack Merridew kneels beside a jungle pool on a deserted island, smearing clay and charcoal across his face. He stares at his painted reflection, then leaps to his feet laughing, a crude mask drawing the eyes of the other boys and appalling them. Behind him the hunters smear their own faces with paint, and the scene crossfades to a modern support office where technician Marcus pulls a hoodie over his head and turns his camera off before joining a team chat.
assets.player_mission: Study Jack's transformation and identify exactly what the painted mask does to his psychological state. Then choose the second condition, in addition to anonymity, that allows the newly masked hunters to commit their first kill.
key_concepts: A simple change in one's external appearance, such as painting the face, can trigger dramatic changes in overt behavior, as in Lord of the Flies.
Jack's painted mask was a thing on its own, behind which Jack hid, liberated from shame and self-consciousness.
After disguising themselves with painted masks, the boys were readily able to kill the pig, cut its throat, and spill its blood.
Anything that makes people feel anonymous, as though no one knows who they are or cares to know, reduces their sense of personal accountability.
Reduced accountability creates the potential for evil action, especially when a situation or agency gives permission for antisocial or violent action.
Anonymity need not produce destructiveness; if a situation conveys reduced self-centeredness and encourages prosocial behavior, people are ready to make love rather than make war.
Golding's insight about anonymity and aggression was psychologically valid, but in more complex and interesting ways than he depicted.
Deindividuation suspends conscience, self-awareness, sense of personal responsibility, morality, guilt, shame, and fear.
In the deindividuated state, what is possible and available dominates what is right and just, and the moral compass of individuals and groups has lost its polarity.
The transition from Apollonian to Dionysian mentalities can be swift and unexpected, making good people do bad things.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests deindividuation: anonymity suspends the cognitive controls that ordinarily restrain behavior, so action comes under the control of immediate situational demands. Golding's choirboys and Zimbardo's research both show that concealing identity lowers personal accountability and unlocks destructiveness when the situation permits it.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Deindividuation is a psychological state in which anonymity reduces the actor's sense of personal accountability, so behavior comes under the control of immediate situational demands rather than conscience. The battle tests whether the player recognizes that the painted mask changed Jack's behavior not by altering his character but by removing the shame and self-consciousness that restrain it.
assets.stage_1_observation: Jack paints his face into a mask and sees his reflection in the water. The text notes that he looked not at himself but at an awesome stranger, and that his laughter became a blood-thirsty snarling as he capered toward Bill.
assets.stage_1_question: What did the mask do to Jack psychologically?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: It conferred anonymity and liberated him from shame and self-consciousness, suspending the restraints of conscience rather than changing his underlying character.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The other boys now wear painted masks too. They chant that they will kill the pig, cut its throat, and spill its blood, and the first kill is about to be accomplished. A second condition is needed for the newly anonymous boys to actually complete this alien deed.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The situation must grant permission for the ordinarily prohibited aggressive act; in the novel, the escalating group hunt and the ritual of the kill provide that permission, so anonymity plus permission together unleash the violence.

assets.topic: The Escalating Shock Gauntlet: Deindividuation in the Lab
assets.visual_frame_description: A dim laboratory corridor: four women in hoods and oversized lab coats sit in adjacent cubicles facing a one-way mirror, each with a shock button. Behind the glass, a young woman in an alleged creativity study twists and moans as a shock light blinks. A control-room monitor displays shock-hold durations creeping upward across twenty numbered trials while the deindividuated women's hands hover over the switches.
assets.player_mission: Compare the hooded and name-tagged groups and determine who delivered longer shocks and why. Then explain what drives the escalation across the twenty trials as the victims twist and moan.
key_concepts: Female college students in a cover story about creativity under stress believed they were delivering painful shocks to two women they could see and hear behind a one-way mirror.
Half the volunteers were made anonymous with hoods, loose oversized lab coats, and numbers instead of names; the other half wore name tags that made them feel unique.
Everything was identical for both groups except the manipulation of anonymity versus identifiability.
Unlike in Milgram's paradigm, there was no authority directly pressuring the students to deliver the painful shocks.
The women in the deindividuation condition delivered twice as much shock to both victims as did the individuated women.
Anonymous women shocked both victims equally, regardless of whether they had rated a target woman as pleasant or unpleasant.
Individuated women discriminated between the targets, shocking the pleasant woman less over time than the unpleasant one.
Shock time increased over the course of the twenty trials, holding the finger down ever longer as the victims twisted and moaned.
The escalation appears to be an upward-spiraling effect of emotional arousal, each action stimulating a stronger, less controlled next reaction.
The experience comes not from sadistic motives of wanting to harm others but from the energizing sense of domination and control over others.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests deindividuation and the self-reinforcing escalation of aggression: anonymity removed the students' sense of personal accountability, so the duration of shock they delivered doubled and climbed across trials. The escalation appears to be an upward-spiraling effect of emotional arousal, each aggressive act energizing a stronger, less controlled next reaction.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Anonymity reduces personal accountability and, absent any authority or conformity pressure, is sufficient to double the severity of harm people inflict. The battle tests whether the player understands both the deindividuation effect and the self-reinforcing escalation of aggression across repeated opportunities.
assets.stage_1_observation: Four hooded women in identical lab coats sit in separate cubicles, each holding a shock button. Behind the one-way mirror a woman in the alleged creativity study squirms in apparent pain. Across the room, four name-tagged women in otherwise identical conditions face the same button and the same two victims.
assets.stage_1_question: Which group delivered longer shocks, and what happened to their behavior over the twenty trials?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The anonymous, hooded women delivered twice as much shock to both victims and held the button down ever longer over the twenty trials, while the individuated women shocked the pleasant target less over time.
assets.stage_2_intervention: One anonymous participant, Dana, is about to finish her second round of twenty trials. The unpleasant target has just been replaced by the pleasant one, yet Dana's finger stays on the trigger just as long. You must decide what is actually driving Dana's behavior.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Dana's aggression is driven by deindividuation plus escalating emotional arousal: her previous liking for the pleasant victim no longer matters once she is anonymous, and the agitated behavior is self-reinforcing, coming from the energizing sense of domination rather than sadistic motives.

assets.topic: The A-B-A Costume Party: Anonymity as Outward Response Change
assets.visual_frame_description: A bright elementary school gymnasium set up as a Halloween party: beanbag tubes, token booths, and a prize table. Children chase each other in costumes, pushing and shoving to grab a single beanbag, while a tally board tracks aggression percentage and a token counter climbs and falls through three phases labeled A, B, A.
assets.player_mission: Track the children's aggression percentages and token counts through the three phases of the A-B-A design. Then predict what the final phase will reveal about the nature of the change that anonymity produced.
key_concepts: Scott Fraser supervised an experimental Halloween party where children won tokens for games, exchangeable for gifts at the end.
Half the games were nonaggressive and half involved confrontations between two children competing to reach a goal, with aggression typically involving pushing and shoving.
Each child served as his or her own control in an A-B-A format: play without costumes, then with costumes, then without costumes again.
Aggression among the schoolchildren increased significantly as soon as they put on the costumes.
The percentage of time children spent in aggressive games more than doubled, from 42 percent in phase A to 86 percent in phase B.
Aggression had a high negative payoff: children earned fewer tokens while acting aggressively, averaging 31 tokens in the anonymous B phase versus 58 in the A phase.
There was no carryover of aggressive behavior from phase B to the final A phase, where aggression dropped to 36 percent and tokens soared to 79.
The behavior change brought on by anonymity did not create a dispositional, internal change, but only an outward response change.
Change the situation, and behavior changes in lockstep fashion.
Aggression became its own reward, with goals that were distant taking a backseat to the fun and games of the present moment.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the A-B-A logic of deindividuation research: the children's aggression rose with anonymity and fell the moment anonymity was removed, proving the change was an outward response to the situation, not an internal dispositional change. When the costume goes, the situation changes, and behavior follows in lockstep fashion.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The A-B-A design uses each child as his or her own control, isolating anonymity as the causal variable. The battle tests whether the player can distinguish a transient, situation-driven response change from a stable dispositional change in character.
assets.stage_1_observation: Without costumes the children play the games normally, with aggression around 42 percent and a steady 58 tokens won. Costumes arrive; the children are dressed in different rooms so their identities are not known to each other, and the same games resume.
assets.stage_1_question: What does the data in the costumed phase show about the effect of anonymity on the children?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Aggression rose sharply to 86 percent and token winnings fell to 31, showing that perceived anonymity dramatically increased aggression even though it cost the children valued prizes.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The costumes are removed, allegedly to be given to children at other parties, and the games continue as in the first phase. You must decide what the final A phase will reveal about the behavior change.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Aggression will drop back to roughly the baseline level, about 36 percent, and tokens will soar to 79, proving there was no carryover and that the change was an outward response to the situation rather than a dispositional change.

assets.topic: The Good Samaritan in a Hurry: Time Pressure and Bystander Inaction
assets.visual_frame_description: A stone-lined alley at Princeton Theological Seminary. A young man in a clerical collar, clutching a folder, hurries past a stranger slumped against the bricks and moaning in clear distress. A clock in the corner ticks, and a video camera waits at the far end of the quad, while a translucent banner overhead reads: the parable of the Good Samaritan, Luke 10.
assets.player_mission: Diagnose why the seminarians failed to stop for a man in clear distress. Then select the situational intervention that reliably converts passive bystanders into helpers.
key_concepts: Seminary students were on their way to deliver a videotaped sermon on the Good Samaritan when they passed a stranger in an alley, on the ground and clearly in need of aid.
The students were randomly assigned to conditions in which they believed they had little time or a lot more time to reach the taping center.
Fully 90 percent of the seminary students passed up the immediately compelling chance to be a Good Samaritan because they were in a hurry to give a sermon about it.
The more time the seminarians believed they had, the more likely they were to stop and help.
The situational variable of time pressure accounted for the major variations in who helped and who were passive bystanders.
The failure to help strangers in distress is more likely due to situational variables than to dispositional inadequacies.
In a replication, when the seminarians were on their way to fulfill a less important task, the vast majority did stop to help.
Rather than callousness, failure to intervene can stem from denying the seriousness of the situation and from fearing doing the wrong thing and looking stupid.
Being part of a passively observing group means each individual assumes that others are available who could or will help.
Personality tests of participants showed no significant relationship between personality characteristics and the speed or likelihood of intervening in staged emergencies.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the situational power of time pressure in bystander intervention: nearly all the seminarians passed by a man in distress because their task demanded speed, not because they lacked compassion. When the situational demand was relaxed, the vast majority stopped to help, showing the passivity was situational rather than dispositional.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests whether the player recognizes that bystander inaction in this study was driven by the situational variable of time pressure, not by callousness of character, and that changing the situation reliably changes helping.
assets.stage_1_observation: A Princeton Theological Seminary student has just been told he is late for his videotaped sermon on the Good Samaritan. On his way across campus he passes a stranger huddled in an alley, moaning and clearly in distress. He keeps walking toward the taping center.
assets.stage_1_question: Why did roughly 90 percent of these seminarians fail to stop for the man in distress?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Because they were in a hurry to deliver their sermon on the Good Samaritan; the situational variable of time pressure, not dispositional callousness, predicted who stopped to help.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The research team reruns the study but changes one feature: some students are told the taping is a low-priority task and they have ample time. You must decide which intervention converts passive seminarians into helpers.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Relaxing the time pressure and lowering the task's importance: in the replication, when seminarians were on their way to a less important task, the vast majority did stop to help.

assets.topic: Bad Apples or Bad Barrel: The Dispositional-Situational Fight over Abu Ghraib
assets.visual_frame_description: A press conference in Washington: a senior official points at a glowing photograph of the Abu Ghraib Tier 1A abuses on a screen behind him, calling the abusers a few bad apples. In the foreground a chart splits into a barrel labeled rotten apples and a barrel labeled bad barrel, with a third pane labeled the System showing military and political command structures.
assets.player_mission: Evaluate the bad-apples framing of the Abu Ghraib abuses and identify its level of causal analysis. Then choose the analysis that the chapter argues the independent investigations support.
key_concepts: The president of the United States vowed to get to the bottom of the Abu Ghraib abuses, while politicians and pundits proclaimed it was all the work of a few bad apples.
The abusers were publicly characterized as nothing more than a band of sadistic rogue soldiers, a standard dispositional analysis.
Zimbardo's plan is to contrast the dispositional analysis of evil perpetrators in an otherwise good barrel with a search for situational determinants, the nature of the bad barrel.
Independent investigations into the abuses take the analysis beyond situational factors to implicate the System, both military and political, in the explanatory mix.
The dispositionalist view puts the big chips on the Person and the chintzy chips on the Situation.
Recognizing common frailties in the face of situational forces is the first step in shoring up resistance to detrimental influences.
The situationist approach gives others the benefit of attributional charity: any deed, for good or evil, that any human being has done, we could also do given the same situational forces.
Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice rejected situational analysis of terrorism as excuse mongering, championing a dogmatic, simplistic dispositional view of evil people.
People in positions of power and authority often reject causal situational analyses in matters of great national concern.
There is a substantial body of evidence from the behavioral sciences about the power of the social context in influencing behavior.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the contrast between dispositional and situational-systemic levels of analysis: labeling Abu Ghraib's abusers as bad apples locates evil inside the perpetrators, whereas Zimbardo's analysis locates the cause in a bad barrel and the broader military-political System. The evidence supports the situationist reading, with independent investigations implicating systemic factors.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests whether the player can distinguish the dispositional bad-apples framing of the Abu Ghraib abuses from the situational bad-barrel and systemic analyses that the chapter's evidence supports.
assets.stage_1_observation: A press conference describes the Tier 1A abuses as the work of a few sadistic rogue soldiers in an otherwise good military. Pundits nod, and a chart on the wall reduces all causes to the moral character of individual military police.
assets.stage_1_question: What level of causal analysis does the bad-apples framing represent?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: A dispositional analysis, which attributes the evil to the internal character of the individual perpetrators rather than to the situation or system that shaped them.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Independent investigations conclude that the abuses cannot be explained by the few photographed military police alone and point to command structures, failed oversight, and authorized policies. You must select the analysis the chapter argues best fits the evidence.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: A situational-plus-systemic analysis: the bad barrel of the prison situation and the broader military-political System, not just the dispositions of a few soldiers, must be included in the explanatory mix.

assets.topic: The Guinea Pig's Payback: Depersonalizing Treatment and Theft
assets.question: Audit the recording of a student who stole coins and pens from a professor's office. What best explains her theft?
assets.visual_frame_description: A psychology professor's cluttered university office: a bowl of coins and a cup of pens sits near the door. A student lingers alone in the room after being dismissed, glancing at the bowl, while a hidden camera feed in the corner shows the same student scooping coins and slipping them into a pocket. A caption below the feed reads: students treated as guinea pigs versus students treated humanely.
assets.player_mission: Audit the hidden-camera footage and the interrogation of the student who stole from the professor's office. Deliver the correct diagnosis of the mechanism behind the theft.
assets.subject_baseline: Deena is a college volunteer who normally behaves courteously toward staff and has no record of stealing; in the humane condition of the study she is greeted by name and treated as a valued individual.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: When left alone in the office, Deena stands near the coin bowl and looks at the door, then at the area where the hidden camera is mounted, her posture tense; she scoops coins quickly, glances at the door again, pockets them, and leaves with an abrupt, slightly hunched stride.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Researcher: Deena, you were alone in my office for a few minutes. Did you touch the bowl of coins or the pens? Deena: No, I just came to drop off the forms. I did not touch anything. Researcher: You seemed nervous when you came out. Is something wrong? Deena: It is fine. This whole experiment made me feel like a lab subject, honestly. What did it matter anyway?
assets.correct_diagnosis: Deena is an anonymous, deindividuated subject: being treated as an undifferentiated guinea pig stripped her sense of personal identifiability, and the situation supplied opportunity, making theft far more likely than for students treated humanely.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Her denial is consistent with the professor's study, where students treated as guinea pigs stole much more often than humanely treated students; her remark that she felt like a lab subject reveals the depersonalizing treatment that conferred anonymity, and the act matches the transgression the experiment documented rather than a pre-existing criminal disposition.
distractors: Deena is a habitual thief who steals whenever opportunity arises, unrelated to how she was treated.
Deena stole because she was directly pressured by an authority figure to take the coins.
Deena stole to help a friend, and the professor's study has nothing to do with her behavior.
key_concepts: Anonymity can be conferred on others not only by masks but also by the way that people are treated in given situations.
When others treat you as if you are not a unique individual but just an undifferentiated other being processed by the System, you feel anonymous.
The sense of a lack of personal identifiability can induce antisocial behavior.
A researcher treated college student research volunteers either humanely or as guinea pigs in an experiment.
Students later found themselves alone in the professor-researcher's office with the opportunity to steal coins and pens from a bowl full of them.
Those in the anonymity condition stole much more often than did the humanely treated students.
Kindness can be more than its own reward.
People are not passive objects buffeted by environmental contingencies; they are active agents capable of influencing the course of events their lives take.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests anonymity conferred through depersonalizing treatment: being processed as an undifferentiated guinea pig removed the student's sense of personal identifiability and accountability, so theft surged. The professor's field study showed that students treated this way stole far more often than those treated humanely, illustrating that kindness can be more than its own reward.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.topic: The Candy Bowl Caper: Anonymity in a Halloween Crowd
assets.question: Audit the trick-or-treating group's transgression. What best explains why the masked group took far more than an identifiable child alone?
assets.visual_frame_description: A suburban porch at dusk on Halloween: a bowl labeled Take one overflows with candy and coins, and costumed children crowd the steps. One group of four children in full masks fills pockets while a homeowner stands at the door; a split-screen shows a lone child in a costume hesitating before taking a single piece after being asked to reveal her identity.
assets.player_mission: Audit the trick-or-treating group's behavior and the child's explanation. Deliver the correct diagnosis of what drove the transgression.
assets.subject_baseline: Nine-year-old twins Mia and Theo know the rule take one and have always obeyed it at previous parties; when asked to reveal their identities behind their masks, they take a single piece each and leave.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: In the group condition, the homeowner stays at the door without asking who the children are; the four costumed kids glance at one another, laugh, and scoop fistfuls of candy and coins; two look back at the porch light before grabbing more, then run off giggling down the street.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Parent: Mia, you know the bowl said take one. Why did you take a whole handful? Mia: Everyone else did, it was just a big bowl. I did not even think about the rule. Parent: But you took the candy even though you did not need it. Mia: Nobody knew it was us anyway. We all looked the same.
assets.correct_diagnosis: The children are in an anonymous group, the condition in which the majority stole; the costumes concealed their identities from the homeowner, and being part of a group of friends amplified the transgression far beyond the level of identifiable children.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: In the field study of more than 700 trick-or-treaters, anonymous groups transgressed at a 57 percent rate, far above the 8 percent rate of nonanonymous children alone, and Mia's own explanation matches the study, since concealment of identity plus group membership drove the stealing.
distractors: Mia is simply a greedy child who would steal in any situation, costumed or not.
The homeowner's direct request to take one gave permission to take the entire bowl.
Mia stole because a friend dared her, and anonymity played no part in her decision.
key_concepts: In a related field study, Halloween trick-or-treaters visited local homes in costumes, where bowls filled with candies and coins were labeled Take one.
Going beyond that limit constituted a transgression, stealing.
In the anonymous condition, the homeowner made it evident that he or she could not tell who the children were.
Among the more than 700 children studied, more transgressions were found when they were in anonymous groups, 57 percent, than when anonymous and alone, 21 percent.
Fewer transgressions occurred when nonanonymous children were alone, 8 percent, than when they were in groups of other nonanonymous trick-or-treaters, 21 percent.
Even when alone and identifiable, the temptation of easy money and delicious treats was too great for some children to pass up.
Adding the full-anonymity dimension turned that singular temptation into an overwhelming passion for most children to take all the goodies they could.
The anonymity of the Halloween context facilitated aggression and transgression even when it worked against the children's immediate interests.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests anonymity and group membership as triggers of transgression: costumed children in anonymous groups stole at a 57 percent rate, versus 8 percent for identifiable children alone. The majority of anonymous group members broke the take-one rule because nobody knew who they were, turning a temptation into an overwhelming passion.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.topic: The Supervisor's Hand: Dehumanizing Labels and Escalating Punishment
assets.question: Audit a supervisor whose shock levels climbed to an average of 7 out of 10. What combination of mechanisms best explains his escalation?
assets.visual_frame_description: A 1970s laboratory room where three male college students sit in a supervisory team wearing headsets, watching a decision panel. On a monitor a shock dial climbs past 7 out of 10 while an intercom crackles with a voice described as an animalistic, rotten bunch. A second screen shows the same setup with a group labeled perceptive, understanding.
assets.player_mission: Audit the supervisor's escalating shock levels and his justifications during the debrief. Deliver the correct diagnosis of the mechanisms operating in his behavior.
assets.subject_baseline: Derek is a junior college volunteer who described himself as kind and averse to conflict; on trial one he selects the same mild shock level as everyone else in all three labeling conditions.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: Derek hesitates on early trials, shifting in his seat; by trial ten his hand moves to the dial without hesitation and sets level 7; he stops watching the decision panel, stares at the shock meter instead, and his shoulders relax as he delivers the punishment.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Interviewer: Your shock levels rose steadily across the trials. Why did you keep increasing them? Derek: They were supposed to be evaluating decisions, and honestly, once I heard they were a rotten bunch of animals, it was easier. It was not like punishing real people. Interviewer: Did you feel personally responsible? Derek: It was the team's average level, so we all shared it.
assets.correct_diagnosis: Derek was dehumanizing his victims and diffusing responsibility: the dehumanizing label animals disinhibited escalating punishment to an average of 7 out of 10, and believing the level was the team's average further lowered his personal accountability.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: In Bandura's experiment, supervisors who punished decision makers labeled an animalistic, rotten bunch delivered the most intense shocks, rising linearly to about 7 out of 10, while the nice group got the least; the highest shocks occurred when participants felt less personally responsible and their victims were dehumanized, exactly Derek's combination.
distractors: Derek is a sadist who enjoyed the pain and would have escalated even with humanely labeled victims.
Derek escalated because an experimenter directly ordered him to increase the shock level on each trial.
The escalating shocks reflect his genuine evaluation of worsening decisions rather than any labeling effect.
key_concepts: Bandura and his students designed an experiment in which 72 male volunteers were divided into three-member supervisory teams.
Supervisors punished the inadequate decision making of other college students on 25 bargaining trials.
The supervisors could choose shock intensity from a mild level of 1 to a maximum level of 10 on any trial.
The decision makers were labeled either an animalistic, rotten bunch, a perceptive, understanding group, or neutrally.
Those labeled animals were shocked most intensively, with shock levels climbing higher and higher to an average of 7 out of the maximum of 10.
On the first trial there was no difference at all between the three treatments; the three groups diverged over successive trials.
Significantly higher levels of shock were given when participants believed the shock level was an average response of their team rather than their personal decision.
Diffusion of responsibility, in any form it takes, lowers the inhibition against harming others.
The very highest levels of shock were administered when participants felt less personally responsible and their victims were dehumanized.
Dehumanization promoted the use of self-absolving justifications, which in turn were associated with increasing punishment.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests dehumanization and the diffusion of responsibility in punishment: the label animals stripped the victims of human status, driving shock levels to an average of 7 out of 10, while believing the level was a team average dissolved Derek's personal accountability. Bandura found the harshest punishment occurred exactly when both dehumanization and diffused responsibility were present.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.topic: Three Unhingers of Restraint: Deindividuation, Dehumanization, Diffusion of Responsibility
assets.question: Classify each evidence item to the mechanism it best demonstrates: deindividuation, in which anonymity reduces personal accountability; dehumanization, in which labels strip human status; or diffusion of responsibility, in which the group spreads the blame.
assets.visual_frame_description: A courtroom-style sorting desk shows three labelled bins: a hooded figure for deindividuation, a label stamp reading dehumanized for dehumanization, and a crowd of identical silhouettes for diffusion of responsibility. Evidence cards slide along a track, each showing a study finding, and the player drags each card into the correct bin.
assets.player_mission: Classify each evidence item to the mechanism it demonstrates: deindividuation, dehumanization, or diffusion of responsibility. Sort all seven rows correctly to clear the matrix.
assets.column_c_label: Diffusion of responsibility (group spreads the blame)

rows.label: Hooded women in lab coats delivered twice as much shock as name-tagged women
Supervisors shocked decision makers labeled animals up to an average of 7 out of 10
The more witnesses present at an emergency, the less likely any one of them intervenes
Costumed children's aggression jumped from 42 percent to 86 percent of play time
GIs who called Vietnamese civilians gooks carried out the My Lai massacre
Shock levels rose when participants believed the level was their team's average
Anonymous trick-or-treaters in groups stole candy at a 57 percent rate

distractors: The hooded women shocked more because an authority commanded them to, not because they were anonymous.
The supervisors' escalation was caused by the poor quality of the victims' decisions, not by labels.
Witnesses failed to help because they personally lacked empathy, unrelated to the size of the group.
assets.explanation: The hooded-women study, the costume party, and the anonymous trick-or-treaters all isolate anonymity as the operative factor, so those rows sort to deindividuation; the animals and gooks labels operate through dehumanization; and the witness and team-average findings operate through diffusion of responsibility.
key_concepts: Deindividuation reduces the cues of social accountability of the actor, making him or her feel anonymous.
Dehumanization occurs whenever some human beings consider other human beings to be excluded from the moral order of being a human person.
Deindividuated women in Zimbardo's study delivered twice as much shock to both victims as did the individuated women.
The presence of others diffuses the sense of personal responsibility of any individual to get involved.
Children's aggression more than doubled, to 86 percent of play time, once they were costumed and anonymous.
The more people who witness an emergency, the less likely any of them will intervene to help.
Behind the My Lai massacre of hundreds of Vietnamese civilians was the dehumanizing gooks label that GIs had for those different-looking Asian people.
Supervisors shocked decision makers labeled animals most intensively, up to an average of 7 out of 10.
Anonymous trick-or-treaters in groups stole candy at a 57 percent rate, versus 8 percent for identifiable children alone.
Anything that makes people feel anonymous, as though no one knows who they are, reduces their sense of personal accountability.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests three mechanisms that suspend moral restraint: deindividuation through anonymity, dehumanization through derogating labels, and diffusion of responsibility through group presence. The chapter shows each mechanism independently raises the potential for harm, and in combination they compound it.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.topic: The Four Faces of Moral Disengagement
assets.question: Each row is a mechanism Bandura identified for disengaging moral self-censure. Sort each to its type: redefining harm as honorable, diffusing or displacing responsibility, or reconstructing the victims as deserving.
assets.visual_frame_description: A war-room situation table shows three columns with banners: honorable deed, not my act, and they deserved it. Cards bearing real phrases from history, such as collateral damage, the team's average, and vermin, drift down the screen, and the player files each into the matching moral-disengagement column.
assets.player_mission: Sort each mechanism of moral disengagement into its correct category: redefining harm as honorable, diffusing or displacing responsibility, or reconstructing the victims as deserving. Assign all seven rows to clear the matrix.
assets.column_a_label: Redefining harm as honorable (justification, euphemism, comparison)
assets.column_b_label: Diffusing or displacing responsibility (not my act)
assets.column_c_label: Reconstructing victims as deserving (blame and dehumanize)

rows.label: We only torture them; they behead us, an advantageous comparison
Using the euphemism collateral damage for civilians bombed into dust
Delivering the shock level as an average of our team, not my personal choice
A Japanese general describing Chinese victims as things, not people like us
Casting Rwandan Tutsis as nothing more than insects and cockroaches
The orders came from higher up, so I am not the agent of this harm
Nazi propaganda portraying Jews as vermin and voracious rats before the genocide

distractors: Moral disengagement requires permanently changing a person's moral standards, not just selectively disengaging self-censure.
Bandura's mechanisms apply only to soldiers and terrorists, not to everyday situations.
Advantageous comparisons and euphemisms are forms of diffusion of responsibility rather than redefining harm.
assets.explanation: Moral justification, advantageous comparison, and euphemistic language all recast the harmful act as honorable, so those rows sort to column a; team-average and orders-from-above framing shift the agent of harm, sorting to column b; and animalizing or blaming the victims reconstructs them as deserving, sorting to column c.
key_concepts: Bandura's model of moral disengagement describes the specific mechanisms people generate to convert harmful actions into morally acceptable ones.
One mechanism redefines harmful behavior as honorable through moral justification, advantageous comparison, and euphemistic language.
Euphemisms such as collateral damage and friendly fire sanitize the reality of cruel actions.
A second mechanism minimizes the sense of a direct link between actions and harmful outcomes by diffusing or displacing personal responsibility.
A third mechanism changes the way people think about the harm done, ignoring, distorting, minimizing, or disbelieving negative consequences.
A fourth mechanism reconstructs victims as deserving their punishment by blaming them and dehumanizing them.
Most people adopt moral standards through socialization, and moral self-censure can be selectively disengaged at certain times and for certain purposes.
Dehumanization promotes the use of self-absolving justifications, which in turn are associated with increasing punishment.
The model helps explain not only political, military, and terrorist violence but also everyday situations in which decent people routinely perform harmful acts.
Understanding these mechanisms is not excusing the behavior; making the mechanisms explicit is a step toward reversing them.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests Bandura's four mechanisms of moral disengagement, which allow people to shift their morality into neutral gear while keeping their moral standards intact. Each mechanism works by redefining the act, severing the actor from the harm, or stripping the victims of worth.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.topic: Three Levels of Causal Analysis: Apples, Barrel, and System
assets.question: Classify each claim by the level of causal analysis it represents: dispositional analysis of the bad apple, situational analysis of the bad barrel, or systemic analysis of institutional and political structures.
assets.visual_frame_description: An evidence wall in a law-enforcement review office displays three framing boxes: a single portrait labelled bad apple, a barrel full of apples labelled bad barrel, and a network of command arrows labelled the System. Headline clippings about Abu Ghraib, Hurricane Katrina, and Milgram's predictions slide across the screen for the player to route to the correct frame.
assets.player_mission: Classify each claim by its level of causal analysis: dispositional, situational, or systemic. Sort all seven rows correctly to clear the matrix.
assets.column_a_label: Dispositional analysis (the bad apple or person)
assets.column_b_label: Situational analysis (the bad barrel or social context)

rows.label: Secretary Rice dismissing situational explanations of terrorism as excuse mongering
Forty psychiatrists predicting only 1 percent of Milgram's participants would reach 450 volts
Situationists granting others the benefit of attributional charity
Independent investigations implicating the military and political System in Abu Ghraib
The prosecution refusing to consider situational forces in the SPE participants' conduct
The Bush administration's nil, too-late response to Hurricane Katrina
Ross and Shestowsky urging the legal system to weigh evidence on the power of social context

distractors: The psychiatrists' low prediction is a dispositional claim about the participants' character.
Blame for Katrina belongs solely to the individual failures of single officials, not to interlocking systems.
Attributional charity means excusing evil acts rather than explaining their situational causes.
assets.explanation: Claims that locate the cause inside the person, such as Rice's evil-people framing and the SPE prosecutor's dispositional view, sort to column a; analyses of social context, the psychiatrists' underestimation, and attributional charity sort to column b; and institutional failures like the Katrina response and Abu Ghraib's command structures sort to column c.
key_concepts: The dispositionalist view puts the big chips on the Person and the chintzy chips on the Situation.
The situationist approach gives others the benefit of attributional charity when analyzing unthinkable acts of evil.
Forty psychiatrists predicted only 1 percent of Milgram's participants would go all the way to 450 volts, vastly underestimating the situational impact of authority.
Politicians and pundits proclaimed the Abu Ghraib abuses were the work of a few bad apples and rogue soldiers.
Independent investigations into Abu Ghraib implicate the military and political System in the abuses.
Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice dismissed situational analyses of terrorism as excuse mongering, insisting these are simply evil people who want to kill.
The Katrina disaster exemplified the failure of multiple, interlocking systems to mobilize resources when action was essential for survival.
Ross and Shestowsky concluded the criminal justice system should not be guided by illusions about dispositions versus situations.
People are both products of their different environments and producers of the environments they encounter.
A meta-analytic review of 100 years of social psychological research found substantial, reliable effect sizes for the power of social situations.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the three levels of causal explanation the chapter contrasts: dispositional analysis of the bad apple, situational analysis of the bad barrel, and systemic analysis of the System. Zimbardo argues the evidence favors situationist and systemic analyses, and that dispositional shortcuts obscure the real causes of evil.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.topic: Why Good Samaritans Stay Put: Situational Forces on Helping
assets.question: Classify each factor by its effect on bystander intervention: does it promote helping, inhibit helping, or is it a dispositional claim that the research refuted?
assets.visual_frame_description: A city street corner rendered as a decision board shows three lanes: a green lane for promotes helping, a red lane for inhibits helping, and a grey lane for refuted dispositional claims. Cards depicting a purse request, a ticking clock, a growing crowd, and a personality-test report travel down the board, and the player routes each card to its correct lane.
assets.player_mission: Classify each factor as promoting helping, inhibiting helping, or a refuted dispositional claim. Sort all seven rows correctly to clear the matrix.

rows.label: Being directly asked to keep an eye on a purse, creating a social obligation
Believing you are late for a scheduled task, as in the seminary study
The idea that New Yorkers are callous by nature and will not help
Being alone or with only one other witness to an emergency
A growing crowd of onlookers, each assuming someone else will act
Denying the seriousness of the situation and fearing looking stupid
The claim that personality traits predict who intervenes in emergencies

distractors: Being in a hurry is a dispositional trait, not a situational feature of the emergency.
Direct requests to guard property had no measurable effect on bystander behavior.
Crowds reliably increase the likelihood that any individual will intervene.
assets.explanation: Direct requests and solitude remove ambiguity and obligation-sharing, promoting help; time pressure, big crowds, denial of seriousness, and fear of error inhibit help through diffusion and worry; and personality-based and callous-New-Yorker explanations are dispositional claims that bystander research refuted.
key_concepts: Latané and Darley's research generated a counterintuitive conclusion: the more people who witness an emergency, the less likely any of them will intervene to help.
Being part of a passively observing group means each individual assumes that others are available who could or will help.
The mere presence of others diffuses the sense of personal responsibility of any individual to get involved.
Failure to intervene can come from denying the seriousness of the situation and from fearing doing the wrong thing and looking stupid.
Personality tests of participants showed no significant relationship between personality characteristics and the speed or likelihood of intervening in staged emergencies.
In Moriarity's demonstration, a direct request to keep an eye on a purse or radio created a social obligation that was honored fully by virtually everyone.
In the seminary study, the more time the students believed they had, the more likely they were to stop and help.
Want help? Ask for it; chances are good that you will get it, even from allegedly callous New Yorkers or other large-city folks.
There is an emergent group norm of passive non-action among groups of passive observers.
New Yorkers are likely to help and will intervene if they are directly asked or when they are alone or with a few others.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the situational determinants of bystander intervention: whether a person helps depends less on their character and more on factors like the size of the crowd, time pressure, ambiguity, and direct requests. Latané and Darley showed the mere presence of others diffuses responsibility, and personality tests failed to predict intervention.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)
